1:
The chapter opens on the very day Haman's lot had marked for the ruin of the Jews, and the witnesses set the scene at its date and its astonishing reversal. The reformed John Gill fixes the calendar plainly: it is now the twelfth month, the month Adar, and the thirteenth day of it, the term appointed by both the decrees. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch survey the whole chapter's shape before its details unfold: on the day appointed by both edicts the Jews assembled in town and province to slay all who sought their hurt, and, supported by the royal officials, inflicted a great defeat upon their enemies; at the queen's desire the fighting in Susa ran a second day, so that the provinces rested on the fourteenth (vv.16-19) and Susa on the fifteenth, and out of those two rest-days the feast of Purim was born.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry frames it as a decisive and open battle: neither side was surprised, both had long notice, and neither could call the other rebel, for both were armed by royal authority. The enemies were the aggressors, hoping by virtue of the former edict to have power over the Jews notwithstanding the latter; the Chaldee paraphrase, he notes, says none appeared against them but Amalekites only, infatuated and hardened like Pharaoh against Israel, to take up arms to their own destruction. Had they sat still and attempted nothing against the people of God, not a hair of their head would have fallen; but they must be meddling, and so rolled a burdensome stone that returned upon them. Yet the day the enemies reckoned would be theirs proved God's day, as in Ps. 37:13; it was turned to the contrary of what was expected, and the Jews had rule over those that hated them.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lifts his eyes from the battle to the providence behind it, marvelling at the number of ordinary-seeming events that concurred to save a people so signally and, to all appearance, so inevitably doomed. None, he says, are ever too low for God to lift up, or too high for God to cast down; and the watching heathen must have observed that the uncontrollable hand of an Almighty Being had wrought for the Jews, a lesson fit to discredit the idolatry of their country. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds the smallest philological touch, that the decree which "drew near" had, more exactly, arrived or come, the same word as at Esther 8:17. The witnesses do not divide; together they present the appointed day of slaughter overturned into a day of rule, the lot of the heathen overruled by the God of Israel.
2:
Now the Jews take the field, and the witnesses watch a whole empire's dread fall upon their enemies. The reformed John Gill notes simply that they gathered themselves together in their cities throughout all the provinces, wherever they lived. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch trace the Hebrew: "in their cities" means the cities in which they dwelt across the king's dominions; to "lay hand" on such as sought their hurt is the same idiom of stretching out the hand to kill used at Esther 2:21 and Esther 3:6; and "no man could withstand them" (as none could stand before Israel in Joshua 10:8) because the fear of them had fallen upon all people. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the phrase to mean that the enemies, though they did take up arms, were easily conquered and destroyed.

Henry, the puritan-evangelical voice, had already drawn out both the human wisdom and the divine hand in it: the Jews gathered in their cities and stood upon their defence, offering violence to none but bidding defiance to all; had they acted separately, family by family, they would have been an easy prey, but in concert they strengthened one another, for forces are strongest combined. And what God did was to strike all people with a fear of them, as the Canaanites were made afraid of Israel in Josh. 2:9, so that men who had hardihood enough to assault them lost courage to press the assault, and the men of might could not find their hands.

Here the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sounds a dissenting note that will deepen later in the chapter. How far the Jews kept strictly to the letter of the edict, standing for their lives only when attacked, is, he thinks, open to doubt. They had the whole executive of the empire on their side (v.3), and to all intents the second edict was taken virtually to repeal the first; being in favour at court and, after their long alarm, full of indignation and a natural desire for vengeance, they were probably resolved to use their opportunity while they had it, and who, he asks, could object, so long as they did nothing against the authorities? That they made a bloody use of it, Ellicott adds, is shown plainly by the numbers of v.16. So the verse yields two readings held in tension: the others hear an embattled people defending their lives, while Ellicott suspects a favoured people pressing an advantage well past the bounds of mere defence.
3:
The verse turns to the Persian officialdom that threw its weight behind the Jews, and the witnesses weigh both the word and the motive. The reformed John Gill lingers on the verb: the rulers of the provinces, the lieutenants, deputies, and officers of the king "blessed" the Jews, countenanced and encouraged them, gave them all the assistance in their power, and, as the word signifies, lifted them up and spoke well of them, or praised them, as the Targum has it. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms the philology from the other side: "helped" is literally "lifted up," the same Hebrew verb rendered "furthered" at Ezra 8:36.

On the reason for this sudden official favour the voices agree. Keil and Delitzsch, reading in the same grammatical-historical vein, note that all the rulers, satraps and governors, and those who did the king's business supported the Jews because the fear of Mordecai had fallen upon them. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fills in the machinery of it: Mordecai, raised to the king's highest confidence and given authority over the whole realm, was a man these officers could not afford to cross, and so they assisted the Jews, no doubt with the very troops under their command, to overthrow those who had availed themselves of the former decree to molest them. And Clarke draws the moral limit that the narrative itself observes: it does not appear that the Jews slew any person who did not rise up to destroy them, a point he refers forward to v.5.

Henry, the puritan-evangelical witness, had pressed the same motive with a preacher's edge. The rulers helped the Jews not because they bore them any kindness, but because the fear of Mordecai was upon them, he having manifestly the countenance of both God and the king. They saw it their interest to befriend Mordecai's friends, for he was not only great in the king's house and caressed by the courtiers, but his fame for wisdom and virtue had gone out through all the provinces, where he was extolled as a great and thriving man, one that waxed greater and greater. Great men may, by their influence, do a great deal of good, Henry observes; many that fear not God will yet stand in awe of them. The witnesses converge on a single picture: an empire's whole apparatus of power tilted, almost overnight, toward the people it had lately been commanded to destroy, and tilted not by love of the Jews but by dread of the Jew who now sat at the king's right hand.
4:
A single sentence explains the whole turn of the officials, "for Mordecai was great in the king's house," and the witnesses pause to measure the man's new eminence. The reformed John Gill spells out the office behind the greatness: Mordecai was set not only over Esther's affairs but was one of the king's counsellors, indeed the chief minister of state. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch keep close to the Hebrew: Mordecai was much esteemed in the king's house, his fame went out through all the provinces, the same idiom of a spreading report used in Joshua 6:27 and Jeremiah 6:24, and "this man Mordecai became continually greater," a participle of unbroken increase like that describing Jehoshaphat in 2 Chron. 17:12.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the rising fame as the engine of the deliverance. It was because Mordecai was looked upon as a thriving man, one that waxed greater and greater, that for fear of him all the king's officers helped the Jews; and Henry turns the observation into a rule of providence: great men may, by their influence, do a great deal of good, for many who fear not God will nevertheless stand in awe of those whom God has raised. The elevation of one faithful Jew to the second seat of the empire becomes, in effect, a wall thrown up around his whole people.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse gains its force from its placement. Where Esther 3:1 had recorded Haman advanced above all the princes, and the terror of that promotion had driven a decree of extermination, here the same language of greatness is transferred to Mordecai, and the terror it inspires runs the opposite way, toward the sparing of the Jews rather than their ruin. The historian, the witnesses let us feel, is quietly balancing his books: the honour Haman grasped at and abused has passed to the man he despised, and with it the power to protect where Haman had power only to destroy. Mordecai's greatness is not told for his own glory but as the visible token that the God who had abased the persecutor has exalted the persecuted, and set him where his very name is a defence to his people. Gill had made the greatness concrete, a man not merely trusted with the queen's affairs but seated among the king's counsellors as chief minister of state; Keil and Delitzsch had made it dynamic, a participle of one growing continually greater, like Jehoshaphat before him. Henry gathers both into a single providence: the influence of one good man, raised high, becomes a shelter for many, since even those who fear not God will stand in awe of him whom God has advanced. The verse thus reads less as a courtier's honour than as a wall thrown up, in the person of Mordecai, around the whole house of Israel.
5:
The narrative states the outcome in a single heavy clause, "the Jews smote all their enemies with the stroke of the sword, and slaughter, and destruction," and the witnesses attend to the weapons and the warrant. The reformed John Gill pictures the arms in hand: some fell by swords, others by clubs and staves and such slaughtering weapons, as the Targum describes. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch parse the grammar of the blow: the verb of smiting with its preposition means to bring a defeat upon someone, as at 2 Samuel 23:10 and Numbers 22:6, and the piling of "sword, slaughter, and destruction" strengthens the notion to its utmost; while "they did what they would unto those that hated them" means they retaliated upon their enemies at their own discretion, precisely the liberty granted them by the counter-decree of Esther 8:11.

That word "discretion" carries the moral question the chapter keeps raising, and the witnesses hold it two ways. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the discretion narrowly and defensively: for all the sweeping language, it does not appear that the Jews slew any person who did not rise up to destroy them, so that the sword fell only on avowed enemies in arms. Henry, the puritan-evangelical voice, agrees that they smote only those they found in arms, none of whom, having marked themselves for the Jews' destruction, escaped.

Yet the very phrase "did what they would" leaves an opening that Ellicott, elsewhere, presses toward vengeance rather than pure defence. The witnesses do not settle the tension here so much as expose it: the same verse that grants the Jews leave to do according to their will can be read as the restrained justice of a people at last permitted to defend themselves, or as a license whose breadth invites excess. What they agree upon is the completeness of the victory. An armed and confederate malice, gathered to cut every Jewish throat, is broken in a day, and the sword that had been whetted against the covenant people turns, by the king's own warrant and God's overruling, upon the heads that raised it. Gill's picture of swords and clubs and staves keeps the scene from any false grandeur, a scattered people armed with whatever lay to hand standing off the neighbours who had risen to butcher them; and Keil and Delitzsch's heaping of the three nouns, sword and slaughter and destruction, measures how total the repulse was, a malice that had counted on easy killing broken utterly in the field, though, as Clarke and Henry are quick to add, only those found in arms felt the edge of it. The reformed and grammatical-historical witnesses together let the plain clause stand as both a record of triumph and a question left for the reader's conscience.
6:
The scene narrows to the capital, where five hundred fell in a single day, and the witnesses ask how so many enemies could be found at the very seat of a court now wholly in the Jews' favour. The reformed John Gill answers first by locating the slaughter: not within the royal palace itself, where it is unthinkable the Jews had so many foes or made so bloody a stroke, but in the city where the palace stood. That five hundred should rise against the Jews so near the court he calls somewhat wonderful; but these, he judges, were men of Haman's faction, enraged at his disgrace and death and headed by his ten sons, who seized on the standing decree to avenge their father, princes, the Targum says, of the house of Amalek. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke shares the wonder plainly: it is strange that in this city, where the king's mind must have been so well known, five hundred could be found to rise in hostility against those whom they knew the king befriended.

The grammatical-historical witnesses steady the geography and the number. Charles Ellicott insists that "the palace" means the whole royal city rather than the palace strictly so called, for even Xerxes would hardly have allowed bloodshed within the palace precincts except by his own direct order. Keil and Delitzsch read it the same way, that in the citadel of Susa the Jews destroyed, in round numbers, five hundred men; and here begin their long note on the curious way the coming names of Haman's sons are written in the Hebrew Bibles, set out one above another to give them prominence and ease their counting, a peculiarity the later Rabbis, as Buxtorf reports, loaded with hidden meanings it was never meant to carry.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley adds only that Shushan here is the city so called, and that the slain were such as the Jews knew would watch every opportunity to destroy them, and might even now be attempting it. The witnesses do not divide. Together they explain the five hundred as the last, desperate rally of a beaten party, the friends and sons of the fallen favourite, unteachable in their hatred, throwing themselves against the people they had meant to exterminate, and perishing in the ruin they had prepared for others. Even at the heart of the empire, under the eye of a king they knew to be their opponent, malice would not learn; and the number of the dead is the measure of how deep the enmity ran.
7:
The historian pauses to name the sons of Haman one by one, Parshandatha, Dalphon, Aspatha, and the witnesses treat the roll as a deliberate and weighty record. The reformed John Gill reads the ten names through to Vajezatha and marks their place in the battle: the sons of Haman the son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews, were slain along with the five hundred men, at the head of whom they stood. They are not stray casualties but the ringleaders of the whole assault, the inheritors of their father's quarrel who had rallied Haman's faction for one last stroke.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fasten on the way the names are set down. In the Hebrew manuscripts and printed Bibles they are written in a single column, one above another, a mode meant originally only to give the ten names prominence and to make them easy to number. The later Rabbis, they note, could not leave so plain a thing alone: some made the arrangement a sign that Haman's house should never rise again from its ruin, others a picture of the ten hanged in a perpendicular line one above the other; and the odd small and enlarged letters in the first, seventh, and tenth names, over which the same scholars puzzled, carry no meaning that can now be recovered, save perhaps that the great letter in the last name was to mark it as the last. Keil and Delitzsch add the detail that binds this verse to the next stage of the story: for all that they might lawfully have done so under Esther 8:11, on the spoil the Jews laid not their hand.

The witnesses do not divide, and the very listing of the names does a quiet work. Haman had schemed to blot out a whole people and to write their destruction into an irreversible law; instead it is his own line that is entered, name by name, into the record of the slain. The ten sons in whom his house was to be perpetuated are cut off in a single day, at the head of the faction they led, and the roll that should have carried his family's honour becomes the register of its extinction. The witnesses let the plain catalogue speak: the enemy of the Jews is answered not only in his own fall but in the fall of all that bore his name. Gill sets the sons at the head of the five hundred, the very captains of the assault, while Keil and Delitzsch set them in the columned list that keeps their names before every later reader; the household raised to perpetuate Haman is instead entered whole into the register of the slain, cut off together in the single day meant for the slaughter of Israel.
8:
The roll continues, Poratha, Adalia, Aridatha, and the witnesses read the unbroken list as the register of a house wholly cut off. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch carry forward their account of the ten names, set out in the Hebrew one beneath another so that not one of them should be lost in the reckoning; the whole seed of Haman, gathered at the head of the rebellion, is named and numbered in its fall, and the historian will close the tally at the tenth, Vajezatha, whose enlarged final letter marks the end of the line. Nothing in the arrangement, they caution, bears the hidden weight the later Rabbis loaded upon it; its plain purpose was to make the ten stand out and be counted.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry preserves the memory that the later Jews wove around these ten names. When on the feast of Purim they read this book, he reports from Buxtorf, they oblige themselves to recite the names of Haman's ten sons all in one breath, without any pause, because they hold that the ten were killed together and all gave up the ghost in the very same moment. Henry passes on, too, the Chaldee paraphrase's darker sequel: when these ten were slain, Zeresh, Haman's wife who had counselled the gallows, fled with seventy more of his children, and afterward begged their bread from door to door, the proud house that had feasted on its own greatness reduced to beggary in the streets.

The witnesses do not divide, and the naming does its silent work. Haman had cast his lot to destroy a nation and to see his own name exalted above every prince; the record answers him by exalting instead the names of his ten sons upon a single fatal page, and then, in the tradition Henry relays, scattering the remnant of his line to wander and to beg. What he purposed against the whole people of God recoils, name by name, upon his own seed; and the catalogue that reads at first like a mere muster of the dead becomes, in the witnesses' hands, the epitaph of the enemy's house, a family that sought to blot out Israel, itself blotted out and dispersed, so that the very reading of the names each year keeps the reversal in perpetual remembrance. Between Keil and Delitzsch, who will not let the Rabbis load the columned names with hidden portents, and Henry, who preserves the living custom those names gave rise to, the verse holds both a scholar's caution and a people's memory. The one insists the arrangement meant only to make the ten stand out and be counted; the other shows what the counting became, a yearly naming, in a single breath, of a house cut off in a single hour.
10:
The tenth name closes the list, and the verse fastens on a single restraint that the witnesses find more eloquent than the slaughter: "but on the spoil laid they not their hand." The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke marks the point where the account first records it and returns to it again at v.16: the Jews laid no hand on the spoil, giving full proof that they sought their own personal safety and not their enemies' property, though the decree in their favour had expressly authorized them to take it under Esther 8:11. His fellow grammatical-historical witness Charles Ellicott notes the same liberty foregone, that this they might have done according to the edict, while John Wesley, the other wesleyan-arminian voice, supplies the motive: they left the goods to the enemies' own children, that it might appear their action sprang not from malice or covetousness but from mere necessity and the great law of self-preservation.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the reasons into a threefold honour. First, the Jews would to the credit of their religion show a holy and generous contempt of worldly wealth, in imitation of their father Abraham, who scorned to enrich himself with the spoils of Sodom. Second, they would make it plain that they had used their interest at court for the saving of their lives and not the raising of their estates, aiming at nothing beyond their own preservation. Third, and most movingly, their commission had empowered them, like their enemies before them, to destroy even the women and little ones (Esther 8:11); but their humanity forbade them to touch these, and so they left the spoil untaken, that the widows and orphans of the slain might have their subsistence, for to strip them, Henry reasons, would be as good as to slay them, taking away their livelihoods as their lives.

The witnesses do not divide, and the abstinence becomes the chapter's quiet crown. Haman's decree had joined plunder to massacre, arming greed as well as hatred (Esther 3:13); the Jews, holding the same power over their foes, refuse the plunder altogether. The self-restraint answers the calumny that had doomed them and displays a people content to be delivered without being enriched, vengeance disarmed of avarice, and victory kept clean of the greed that had first sought their ruin. Clarke and Wesley read the restraint as evidence of motive, Ellicott grants the liberty they declined, and Henry crowns it with mercy toward the widows and orphans of the slain; the several readings meet in one portrait of a people who would take their lives back and nothing more. The thrice-noted abstinence, marked here and again at the two later tallies, becomes the moral signature of the whole day's work.
11:
The day's reckoning is carried to the throne, and the witnesses divide over the spirit in which it was brought. The reformed John Gill offers two possibilities. The number of those slain in Shushan the palace was laid before the king either by his own order, that he might know how many enemies the Jews had in the city and how many of his subjects had fallen; or else officiously, by others who reported it with the intention of irritating the king against the Jews and turning his favour. Gill does not decide between the two, and the ambiguity is itself instructive: the same report might be an honest accounting or a malicious whisper, according to the heart that carried it.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch simply record the fact and its sequel: on that day an account was given to the king of the result of the conflict and the number slain in Susa, and this became the occasion of his turning to Esther with a fresh and open question. Henry, the puritan-evangelical voice, reads the same moment as evidence that the king continued in his tender concern for the queen: he took account of the numbers put to the sword the first day, told them to Esther, and asked her what more she desired, plainly ready to grant whatever she should name.

The witnesses do not finally divide, for whatever the messenger's motive, the report does the queen's work rather than her enemies'. If it was meant to stir the king against the Jews by the sheer weight of the slaughter, it fails utterly; the number that might have alarmed a hostile prince only prompts a favourable one to offer Esther still more. The verse thus turns on the same providence that has governed the whole book: a fact that could have been used to accuse the Jews is made, in the hand of God, the doorway to their fuller deliverance. What is laid before the king to move him one way moves him the other, and the counting of the dead in Susa becomes the occasion not of a check upon the Jews but of the second day's leave that Esther is about to ask. Gill's two motives for the report, honest reckoning or malicious mischief, and Keil and Delitzsch's plainer note of the account simply given, together leave the messenger's heart in shadow; but the outcome is not in doubt. Henry hears in the king's ready telling of the numbers to Esther the same tenderness that had held out the sceptre, and the witnesses agree that whatever hand carried the tally to the throne, it served only to open the door wider for the queen.
12:
The king breaks his own astonishment into a question, and the witnesses hear in it both his wonder and his unwearied favour. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch give the sense of his words: the Jews have slain five hundred men and the ten sons of Haman in the citadel of Susa alone; "what have they done in the rest of the king's provinces?" That is, if five hundred fell in the capital, how many may not have fallen through the length of the empire? The number staggers even Ahasuerus; yet, far from recoiling, he turns at once to Esther with the same boundless offer he had twice made before, at the sceptre and at the banquet, "now what is thy petition? it shall be granted thee," the very language of Esther 5:6 and Esther 7:2.

The reformed John Gill sets the exchange in its moment, after the account had been brought in to him; and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws out the king's temper in the words. By "what have they done in the rest of the provinces" the king means that there, doubtless, many more were slain; and his drift, Wesley paraphrases, is generous to the last: so that I have fully granted thy petition, and yet, if thou hast anything farther to ask, I am ready to grant it. The king reckons the great slaughter not as a thing to be checked but as the measure of how completely he has already given Esther her desire, and offers still more atop it.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse quietly measures the distance the book has travelled. The king who once sold a whole people to Haman for destruction, sealing it with his ring, now recites their enemies' death-toll to the queen as a satisfaction and presses her to name a further wish. The same royal caprice that had made Ahasuerus so dangerous an instrument in Haman's hand makes him now, under God's overruling, a pliant instrument of deliverance. What Esther will do with so open a door the next verse tells; but the witnesses mark first the wonder of the door itself, an absolute king laying his power, a third time, at the feet of the Jewish queen whose people his own decree had condemned. Keil and Delitzsch measure the king's astonishment in his own question, Gill fixes the moment after the account was in, and Wesley hears in the words a generosity that reckons the great slaughter itself as proof of how fully the queen's wish was met. The witnesses let the third renewal of the boundless offer stand as the book's quiet marvel, a capricious despot bent, at every turn, to the deliverance of the people he had signed away.
13:
Given leave to ask, Esther asks for a second day of fighting in Susa and for the bodies of Haman's ten sons to be hung upon the gallows, and here the witnesses openly divide, more sharply than anywhere else in the book. The reformed John Gill notes only her submission, "if it please the king," for she was all deference to his will. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley defends the request as sober necessity: the leave to fight another day was to reach their implacable enemies, for it is likely the worst and greatest of them had hidden themselves through the thirteenth, meaning to return in safety once the Jews' commission had expired; and the hanging of the ten already slain was for their greater infamy and the terror of all who should presume to abuse the king or urge such cruelties again. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it the same practical way, that the sons, killed the day before, were now to be exposed on posts or gibbets as a warning to any who still sought the Jews' destruction.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry is at pains to clear the queen of cruelty: Esther was surely none of the blood-thirsty, none who delight in slaughter, but had some very good reasons that moved her; she sought the utter crushing of a malignant party, and asked that the dead sons be hanged for the greater disgrace of their father's house and the terror of his faction, it being supposed they were left hanging in chains for a time.

Against all these stands the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott, who refuses to soften what he sees. It seems to him impossible to acquit Esther of simple blood-thirstiness: before the first day's slaughter was even over the Jews were plainly in no danger, the court's sympathies were known to be wholly theirs, and a second day of killing was therefore, he says flatly, needless butchery. The request to hang sons already dead (v.10) he calls a gratuitous outrage upon the dead. Because Esther was God's chosen agent, he argues, we are not obliged to explain away the black spots in her history; yet neither should we judge her by the high Christian standard, for though the Old Testament taught "vengeance is mine," it needed the teaching of the New to bring that truth home. So the debate stands unresolved: was Esther's second petition the righteous completing of a necessary defence, or an act of vengeance that even her admirers must own as a stain? The others plead her cause; Ellicott, alone, enters the charge against her.
14:
The king grants both parts of the queen's request, and the witnesses take care to distinguish exactly what the new decree covered. The reformed John Gill reads it simply as leave for the Jews to seek out and slay the rest of their enemies in Shushan on the fourteenth day, just as they had on the thirteenth. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch press a nicety the English blurs: "the decree was given at Shushan; and they hanged Haman's ten sons" does not mean the decree concerned the hanging. The order given in Susa refers rather to the permission to fight against their enemies on the morrow, a reading required both by comparison with Esther 8:13 and by the flow of the verse, since it is in consequence of this decree that the Jews assemble again on the fourteenth (v.15); the hanging of the sons is added only in a trailing clause, a bare accomplished fact.

The distinction matters more than a grammarian's scruple. It keeps the second day from being a second sentence of death upon the ten, who were already dead; the gibbet does no fresh killing but only exposes the slain, while the fresh decree does its real work in loosing the Jews to defend themselves one day more. So the witnesses guard against the very reading that would make Esther's request bloodier than it was: the new grant multiplies not executions but a day of lawful defence, and the hanging is a public shaming of corpses, not a killing of the living.

Neither Gill nor Keil and Delitzsch quarrel over the fact; they differ only in emphasis, the one content with the plain leave to fight, the other anxious that the reader not misread the decree as a warrant for the gallows. Together they let the verse turn the king's easy compliance into two distinct things, a day and a spectacle, and set the stage for the shorter, sharper action of the fourteenth, when three hundred more of the faction that would not disband are cut down in the streets of the capital. Henry adds that the thing was done accordingly, the bodies of the ten exposed, it is supposed hanging in chains and left so for a time, that the disgrace might be public and the terror lasting. So the witnesses let the king's brief command carry its two weights without confusing them: Gill sees the plain leave to fight, Keil and Delitzsch guard the grammar that keeps the decree from meaning the gallows, and Henry supplies the grim spectacle that followed. The fourteenth is opened for defence, and the corpses of Haman's house are made a warning that malice against the Jews had found its wages.
15:
On the added day the Jews of Susa take the field again, and the witnesses tally the result. The reformed John Gill notes only that they gathered on the fourteenth as they had on the thirteenth. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch record the count: on this second day the Jews slew three hundred more, again laying no hand on the spoil, just as at v.10. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke adds the reckoning and its cause: Esther had probably been told by Mordecai that many enemies who sought the Jews' destruction had escaped the first day's fighting, and so begged this second day; the leave being granted, three hundred more were found, eight hundred in Susa altogether, and thus, Clarke concludes, the capital was purged of all its enemies.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott offers a small correction of the rendering, that the verse should open not "for the Jews" but simply "and the Jews," a connective that ties the second day plainly to the first rather than making it a reason for what precedes. The point is minor, but it belongs to his careful reading of a chapter he watches with a critical eye; and it leaves the fact untouched, that the Susa Jews fought two days where the provinces fought but one.

The witnesses do not divide over the numbers, and their agreement quietly answers the charge that hangs over the second day. If, as Clarke and Wesley hold, the worst of the faction had hidden themselves on the thirteenth to strike once the Jews' warrant lapsed, then the three hundred cut down on the fourteenth were no innocents caught in an excess of zeal but the very enemies who had gone to ground; and the same restraint that had marked the first day marks the second, for again the Jews touch none of the plunder. The capital is cleared, the last of Haman's rally is broken, and the deliverance of Susa is sealed, bought, the witnesses are careful to note, with the lives of avowed foes only, and enriched by not a single confiscated coin. Gill marks the second gathering, Keil and Delitzsch the count of three hundred with the spoil again untouched, Clarke the total of eight hundred by which Susa was wholly purged, and Ellicott the small mending of the opening word; the witnesses combine into a single tidy accounting of the capital's last day of danger. What began as a decree of annihilation ends, in Susa, with the faction of Haman broken to the last man who would take up arms, and with the delivered people richer by nothing but their own preserved lives.
16:
The eye widens from the capital to the whole empire, where the Jews of the provinces defend themselves in a single day, and the witnesses weigh the great number that falls. The reformed John Gill notes that they gathered in a body, in their several provinces and cities. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch give the sum and its frame: the Jews stood for their lives, had rest from their enemies, and slew of their foes seventy-five thousand, but laid no hand on the spoil. They observe that the phrase of resting from their enemies is set oddly early, before the slaughter is fully told, because the narrator wished at once to point to how the whole matter ended, in rest.

Henry, the puritan-evangelical witness, reads the number through the ancient quarrel it closed: if all these were Amalekites, as the Jews suppose, then surely now was fulfilled the sentence that the remembrance of Amalek should be utterly blotted out, as in Exod. 17:14; and what justified the Jews in an execution so vast was that they did it in their own necessary defence, standing for their lives by the law of self-preservation as well as by the king's decree. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott, more troubled, records that the Septuagint gives the number as fifteen thousand, which he thinks perhaps the more probable figure, and gathers from Bishop Wordsworth a wider reflection: the whole history shows the recklessness of human life that prevailed among the sovereigns of the great Eastern nations, and displays what ruin would have followed for civilization had Ahasuerus, that is Xerxes, triumphed at Salamis, Oriental ruthlessness and polygamy overrunning the West. The same hand of God, Wordsworth concludes, wrought for the deliverance of mankind at Salamis and Plataea as truly as for the preservation of the Jews in the provinces of Persia.

The witnesses do not divide over the essential thing. Whether the slain were seventy-five thousand or fifteen, whether the Persian records or the Greek preserve the truer count, all agree that a scattered and defenceless people, marked for extinction across a hundred and twenty-seven provinces, stood their ground in a single day and came through into rest, and that the rest, not the slaughter, is where the narrator means the reader's eye to come to settle. Gill's body of provincial Jews, Keil and Delitzsch's early word of rest, Henry's blotting out of Amalek, and Ellicott's troubled arithmetic with Wordsworth's grand reflection all converge on that one settled point. The number may be disputed and the wider history invoked, but the shape of the verse is fixed: a people gathered for their lives across the whole empire, and, when the killing was done, brought at last into rest.
17:
The verse gathers the provincial victory into a date and a rest, and the witnesses read the resting as the true point of the day. The reformed John Gill ties the words back to what precedes: "on the thirteenth day of the month Adar" belongs with the sixteenth verse, marking the day on which the Jews of the provinces gathered and slew so many thousands of their enemies; and on the fourteenth they rested and made it a day of feasting and gladness.

Henry, the puritan-evangelical voice, dwells on the choice of the day kept. Observe, he says, that they kept as their festival not the day on which they fought but the day on which they rested; and here he finds the pattern of the sabbath itself, appointed not on the day God finished his work but on the day he rested from it. The provincial Jews cleared themselves of their enemies on the thirteenth and rested on the fourteenth, and it was that day of rest, not the day of battle, which they set apart for thanksgiving. Both they and the Jews of Susa, Henry notes, celebrated their festival the very day after they had finished their work and gained their point.

From this Henry draws the practical lesson the witnesses let stand as the verse's fruit: when we have received signal mercies from God, we ought to be quick and speedy in our thankful returns to him, while the mercy is fresh and its impression upon the heart is most keenly felt. The Jews lost no time; the sword was scarcely sheathed before the feast was spread. The witnesses do not divide, and the verse quietly instructs by its very calendar, that deliverance is completed not in the striking down of enemies but in the rest that follows, and that the rest is to be filled at once with gladness and the praise of the God who gave it. The day of blood becomes, on its morrow, a day of bread and rejoicing, and it is the morrow, not the battle, that Israel is bidden to remember. Gill ties the date back to the great provincial slaughter of the verse before, and Henry draws from the choice of the rest-day both the pattern of the sabbath and a rule for the grateful heart, that thankful returns should be swift while the mercy is warm. The witnesses do not divide, and the verse instructs by its calendar alone: Purim will keep, not the anniversary of the sword, but the anniversary of the sheathing of it, dated from rest, and the rest filled with the praise of the God who gave a victory the Jews had done nothing to deserve.
18:
The verse sets the capital's timetable beside the provinces', and the witnesses mark the difference that will shape the feast. The reformed John Gill explains that the Jews of Shushan assembled to defend themselves and destroy their enemies on both the thirteenth and the fourteenth days of Adar, having the decree renewed for the second day as they had held it for the first. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke states it plainly: these two days they were employed in slaying their enemies, and they rested on the fifteenth.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott draws out the consequence for later ages: because the Jews of the capital rested only on the fifteenth, both the fourteenth and the fifteenth are now kept as the festival of Purim, the fourteenth being the chief day. The single day's difference between city and country, the one fighting twice and resting late, the other fighting once and resting early, is thus written permanently into the two-day shape of the feast.

The witnesses do not divide, and the small discrepancy of dates turns out to carry the whole rationale of Purim's double observance. What might look like an untidy accident of history, that the same deliverance ended on different days in different places, becomes the reason the Jews keep not one day but two, the fourteenth for the provinces and the fifteenth for Susa, so that the feast itself remembers both the scattered communities and the embattled capital. The narrator, the witnesses let us see, is not merely recording when the fighting stopped but laying the foundation for a festival whose very calendar preserves the memory of how, and where, the rest was won. The days of killing are numbered and closed; the days of rest are numbered and kept. Keil and Delitzsch set the capital's fuller labour beside the provinces': the Jews of Susa were fighting still on both the thirteenth and the fourteenth, and did not rest until the fifteenth, which they therefore made their day of rejoicing, while the country towns, resting a day earlier, kept the fourteenth. Henry marks the same doubling, that those in Shushan kept the fifteenth and both days were observed, and that in every case the festival fell on the day of rest and not the day of battle. So the witnesses let the small unevenness of the two timetables become the frame of the feast, not a single anniversary but a pair of them, the fourteenth and the fifteenth, keeping between them the memory of both the scattered provinces and the besieged capital, and it is these that the following verses will fix into a perpetual ordinance for the whole people.
19:
The verse explains why the country Jews keep the fourteenth, and the witnesses unfold both the custom and the charity in it. The reformed John Gill relays the rule from Jarchi: those of the villages, who dwell in unwalled towns, observed the fourteenth, while walled towns, like Shushan, kept the fifteenth; and the walls in question, by the Jewish canons, are those standing from the days of Joshua the son of Nun, so that any place walled since his time reads the book of Esther on the fifteenth and any unwalled on the fourteenth, Susa alone keeping the fifteenth though unwalled, because in it the miracle was wrought. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds the philology: the words for "villages" and "unwalled towns" are virtually the same Hebrew term, meaning country towns undefended by bulwarks, the very word set in contrast with "fenced cities" at Deuteronomy 3:5.

Keil and Delitzsch, the other grammatical-historical witnesses, simply record the observance, the fourteenth made a day of gladness and feasting, a good day, and of sending portions one to another, and pass on to the letters by which Mordecai would soon fix the custom for all. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lingers over the sending of portions and gives it a generous turn: the rich sent portions of the sacrifices slain on the occasion to the poor, that they too might be able to keep the day as a festival, so that, as the former sorrow had been general, the joy might be general also.

The witnesses do not divide, and together they make the verse the seedbed of the feast's enduring character. Purim is fixed here not merely as a day of private gladness but as a day of shared bread, in which the deliverance of the whole people is celebrated by seeing that none of the people is left out of the rejoicing. The distinction of walled and unwalled town, which might seem a dry point of rabbinic law, only multiplies the days on which that generosity is practised; and the sending of portions and gifts, which the coming verses will make a standing part of the observance, is already present in this first spontaneous keeping of the day. The joy that God has given is not to be hoarded, the witnesses let us feel, but distributed, measured out to the poor as freely as the mercy was measured out to all. Gill's rule of the walled and unwalled towns, Ellicott's philology of the country places, Keil and Delitzsch's bare record of the day, and Clarke's picture of the rich sending portions to the poor together make the fourteenth a day at once of memory and of mercy, the gladness of the delivered overflowing to the needy among them.
20:
Mordecai now takes up the pen, and the witnesses turn from the battle to its record and to the question of who wrote the book we read. The reformed John Gill takes "these things" to mean the transactions of the two days and their causes, together with the letter that follows; some conclude from this that Mordecai was the penman of the whole book, and so he may have been, Gill allows, though it does not necessarily follow. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reasons that Mordecai's own authorship may extend only thus far, what follows being perhaps added by Ezra or the men of the Great Synagogue, or else that "these things" refers only to the letters he sent the provinces; from here to the end, he observes, is a recapitulation of the history and an account of the appointing of the feast of Purim.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the writing in a striking comparison. If this book be indeed Mordecai's, he cannot but observe the difference between his style and Nehemiah's: Nehemiah at every turn notices the good hand of his God upon him, while Mordecai never so much as mentions the name of God in the whole story. Nehemiah wrote at Jerusalem, where religion was in fashion; Mordecai wrote at Shushan, where policy reigned more than piety, and he wrote after the genius of the place, a warning, Henry adds, that even those with the root of the matter in them may lose the savour of religion when they converse wholly with the worldly. Yet he will not despise the man for it: we may learn from Mordecai that some are truly devout though they do not abound in the shows of devotion, and so we must not judge our brethren. Because so little of the language of Canaan appears in the book, Henry notes, many think Mordecai did not write it, but that it was drawn from the journals of the kings of Persia.

The witnesses do not divide sharply, and their several guesses circle one modest certainty: whoever held the pen, the deliverance was to be written down and dispersed among all the Jews, near and far, that a story they had lived through in fragments might be preserved whole. The purpose of the writing, all agree, was not the author's fame but the people's memory, that the wonder God had wrought should be handed on, and that later generations might set their hope in him.
21:
The letters have a single aim, to make a spontaneous gladness into a settled ordinance, and the witnesses trace how the two days were fixed. The reformed John Gill reads "to stablish this among them" as the making of a permanent thing, annually observed in all future generations, out of what the Jews had now done of their own accord. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch give the substance of the appointment: that they should keep the fourteenth day of Adar and the fifteenth day yearly, as the days on which the Jews rested from their enemies and the month was turned for them from sorrow to joy and from mourning into a good day.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott catches an exactness in Mordecai's decree. The Jews of the provinces had already, of themselves, made the fourteenth a day of gladness; what Mordecai's letter now adds is that the fifteenth also should be so kept, binding the two communities, the country and the capital, to honour both days alike, so that neither the provinces' day nor Susa's should be forgotten by the other.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse marks the moment a deliverance becomes a discipline. The rest that had fallen out differently in different places is here gathered up and imposed as one common observance, that the whole people might remember together. What was born of relief and gratitude in a single year is to be repeated every year, lest the memory fade with the generation that felt it; and the very doubling of the days, far from confusing the feast, ensures that both halves of the story, the scattered provinces and the besieged capital, are carried forward in the keeping of it. The witnesses let the verse do its quiet founding work: an annual, fixed, and shared remembrance is laid down, so that the turning of sorrow into joy should be not a memory of the moment but an inheritance of the nation. Henry marks the season of it too, that the two days fall in the twelfth month, just a month before the passover, so that the first and last months of the year alike keep the memory of the times when God preserved his people; and the Jews kept two whole days together as thanksgiving, thinking them not too much to spend in praising God. Gill's permanence, Keil and Delitzsch's turning of the month from sorrow to joy, and Ellicott's careful adding of the fifteenth all serve the one design, a deliverance made into a discipline, an annual and shared remembrance laid down for every generation to come.
22:
The verse names the reason and the shape of the feast at once, the days on which the Jews rested and the month that turned from sorrow to joy, and the witnesses draw out each mark of the observance. The reformed John Gill glosses the ground of it: these were the days wherein the Jews rested from their enemies, having slain all who rose up to assault them, so that the keeping of the days is a keeping of the rest, not the war. Keil and Delitzsch, the grammatical-historical voices, set out the fourfold command that follows: to make them days of feasting and joy, and of sending portions one to another, and of gifts to the poor, the month that was turned from sorrow to gladness answered by a gladness deliberately shared.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry expounds the three duties as a little pattern of sanctified joy. First, a day of cheerfulness, feasting and joy, for a feast is made for laughter, as in Eccl. 10:19, and when God gives cause to rejoice, why should we not express our joy? Second, a day of generosity, sending portions one to another in token of mutual respect and love, friends having their goods in common. Third, a day of charity, sending gifts to the poor, not to our rich neighbours only but to the poor and the maimed, after the counsel of Luke 14:13; for those who have received mercy must show mercy, and thanksgiving and almsgiving should ever go together, that when we bless God the heart of the poor may rejoice with us.

The witnesses do not divide, and together they make the verse the charter of Purim's peculiar temper. The joy commanded is not a private indulgence but a bond: it knits the delivered people to one another by the exchange of portions, and it reaches beyond the comfortable to the needy by the gifts to the poor, so that the whole community, rich and poor alike, is drawn into a single thanksgiving. Gill grounds the days in the rest from enemies, Keil and Delitzsch lay out the fourfold command of feasting, joy, portions, and gifts, and Henry expounds each as a form of sanctified gladness. The reversal God has wrought, from mourning to a good day, is to be commemorated not by mere merriment but by a generosity that mirrors the mercy received, cheerfulness and open-handedness and charity bound into one; the feast remembers grace by dispensing it, so that when the delivered bless God the heart of the poor may rejoice with them, in the very pattern Henry draws from the counsel to feast the poor and the maimed.
23:
The people ratify what their leaders proposed, and the witnesses attend to the nature of the obligation they took on. The reformed John Gill is careful about its character: the Jews engaged to keep these two days annually as festivals, yet not in a religious but in a civil way, not as parts of divine worship or additions to the law of Moses, but by way of commemorating a civil benefit received. And he records that even so the observance did not pass without scruple: in later times some were troubled by it as an innovation, there being, by one account, eighty-five elders, more than thirty of them prophets, who were distressed over the matter, fearing that to institute a new feast was to add to what God had appointed.

Keil and Delitzsch, the grammatical-historical witnesses, read the verse as the people's confirming of Mordecai's proposal: the Jews undertook to do as they had begun, for they had begun, of themselves, by keeping both days, and as Mordecai had written to them, agreeing in consequence of his letters to make the annual custom binding. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke stresses the perpetuity of the pledge: they had already kept the fifteenth, and some of them the fourteenth, and now, at Mordecai's writing, bound themselves and their successors and all their proselytes to celebrate it every year throughout their generations, a pledge, Clarke notes, that has in fact been kept in all the places of their dispersion, from that day to the present, without any interruption.

The witnesses do not divide, and their several emphases combine into a rounded account. Purim is a human institution, not a divine one, Gill will not let it be mistaken for a holy day of God's appointing, and yet it is undertaken by the whole people with such solemn consent that it has outlasted empires. The very scruple Gill records only underscores the point: the Jews knew the difference between what God commands and what a grateful nation ordains, and they kept Purim in full awareness that it belonged to the second order. Gill weighs the character of the pledge and even the later scruple of the eighty-five elders, Keil and Delitzsch the people's confirming of what they had of themselves begun, and Clarke the unbroken keeping of it in every place of the dispersion down to the present day. That a commemoration so carefully distinguished from worship should nevertheless have been observed unbroken for millennia is, the witnesses let us feel, its own quiet testimony to the greatness of the deliverance it remembers.
24:
The letters rehearse the reason for the feast by naming the enemy and his lot, and the witnesses follow the recapitulation. The reformed John Gill states the plot in a sentence: Haman the son of Hammedatha, the Agagite, the enemy of all the Jews, had formed a design to exterminate them from the whole Persian empire in one day. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch retrace the same ground, that Haman had devised against the Jews to destroy them and had cast Pur, that is the lot, to consume and to destroy them, and note that the verb for their intended destruction is the strong word used mostly of the discomfiture with which God himself routs his enemies, as at Exodus 14:24 and Deuteronomy 2:15. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott simply refers the word Pur back to its first explanation at Esther 3:7, where Haman had cast lots to find his fatal day.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse works by a deliberate irony the letters mean to fix in memory. The very word chosen to name the feast, Purim, from Pur, the lot, enshrines the instrument of Haman's plot; the heathen device by which he sought to fix the most favourable day for a massacre becomes the standing name of the day of Jewish triumph. The lot he cast to consume Israel is turned into the title of Israel's deliverance, so that every yearly keeping of Purim pronounces, in a single Persian word, the overthrow of the scheme it recalls.

That the destroying-word Keil and Delitzsch mark should be one so often used of God's own routing of his foes only sharpens the reversal. Haman had purposed against the Jews the kind of ruin God brings upon the enemies of his people; and the ruin recoiled, by the disposing of the lot that Haman trusted, upon Haman's own head. The witnesses let the recapitulation stand as the ground of the feast: the Jews remember, and teach their children to remember, precisely what was devised against them, that they may the better know from what, and by whom, they were saved. Gill's one-sentence rehearsal of the plot, Keil and Delitzsch's note that the word of destruction is the very word for God's routing of his own enemies, and Ellicott's pointer back to the casting of the lot together sharpen that irony: Haman purposed against Israel the ruin God reserves for his foes, and by the lot he trusted it fell upon himself, so that the very name of the feast pronounces his overthrow. The recapitulation is thus no idle repetition but the ground of the whole observance, teaching each generation the depth of the danger, that it may measure the greatness of the rescue.
25:
The recapitulation reaches its turning-point, the plot recoiling upon its author, and the witnesses divide over a single pronoun. The reformed John Gill reads it of the queen: "when Esther came before the king," to request of him her own life and the life of her people, the king commanded by his letters that Haman's wicked device should return upon his own head. But the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch object that the Hebrew says rather "when it, the matter, came before the king," for Esther is not named anywhere in the context; on the coming of the affair to the king's notice he gave the written order (Esther 8:8) that the plot should fall on Haman's own head, and they hanged him and his sons upon the tree.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott presses the same point from the grammar of the English as well: the word "Esther" is printed in italics because it is not in the Hebrew, which reads literally "and on her, or its, coming"; and to make the pronoun refer to Esther seems harsh, since she has not been mentioned for some time. He therefore prefers, with Keil and Delitzsch, to take it impersonally, "when it, the matter, came before the king." So the witnesses stand divided: Gill hears the verse recall the brave approach of the queen who risked her life, while the two grammatical-historical voices hear only the impersonal coming of the affair to the royal attention.

The difference is small in the telling but real, and the witnesses do not force it to a resolution. On either reading the substance is the same: the device Haman framed against the Jews was, by the king's letter, turned back upon himself, and he and his sons died upon the gallows he had built. Whether the verse credits the reversal to Esther's coming or to the matter's coming, it credits the outcome to the same overruling justice that makes a man's mischief return upon his own head. The witnesses let the grammatical dispute stand without letting it obscure the theology the letters mean to preserve, that the snare was sprung upon the setter, and the enemy of the Jews perished by his own contrivance. Gill hears in the verse the brave coming of the queen, Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott the impersonal coming of the matter to the king's notice; but all three read the same recoil, the wicked device returning by the king's own letter upon Haman's head, and himself and his sons upon the tree he had raised. Whether the pronoun points to Esther or to the affair, the verse fastens the reader's eye on a single law of providence, that the mischief a man frames for the innocent comes home at last to the framer. The grammar divides the witnesses; the justice unites them.
26:
Now the name of the feast is fixed, and the witnesses gather around the word and the reason for its keeping. The reformed John Gill explains it plainly: they called these days Purim, after the name of Pur, the lot, because of the lots that Haman had cast. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley agrees that Pur is the Persian word for a lot, so named because Haman had by lot determined the time of the Jews' destruction, a time God overruled to their triumph. Clarke, the other wesleyan-arminian voice, adds that Haman cast lots to find both the month and the day most favourable for his design, and that the letter here recalled as already seen is Mordecai's, sent in v.20.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch trace the twofold logic of the verse: the first "therefore" gives the reason for the name, drawn from the lot; the second opens the explanation of how these days came to be a general observance among all Jews, namely, for two reasons together, the written injunction of Mordecai and the thing they had themselves experienced. On both grounds the Jews established and took upon themselves, and upon their descendants and all who should join them, inviolably to keep the two days. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms that Purim is still observed on the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar, the day before kept as a fast, and that the whole book of Esther is read through in the synagogue, a custom traceable back to the Christian era, as Josephus and the Mishna attest.

Henry, the puritan-evangelical witness, had drawn the theology out of the name itself: the feast is called Purim from the lot, to remind Israel of the sovereign dominion of the God at whose disposal the lot is, who served his own purposes by the foolish superstitions of the heathen and outwitted the diviners in their own craft, frustrating the tokens of the liars, as in Isaiah 44:25. The witnesses do not divide. Together they make the name a standing sermon: Haman trusted the lot to choose his day of slaughter, but the whole disposing of the lot is of the LORD; and so the feast that carries the heathen word for chance proclaims, year by year, that nothing in the fate of God's people is left to chance at all. Gill and Wesley trace the name to the lot, Clarke to the double casting for month and day, Keil and Delitzsch to the twofold ground of Mordecai's letter and the people's own experience, and Ellicott to the enduring custom of reading the whole book each Purim; Henry alone draws the theology to its point, that the God at whose disposal the lot lies outwitted the diviners in their own craft. The witnesses leave the name of the feast as its own standing sermon.
27:
The people bind not only themselves but their posterity and their converts, and the witnesses mark the reach of the pledge. The reformed John Gill reads it as a solemn undertaking: the Jews appointed the two days as festivals and engaged for themselves, for their children, and for all such as should join themselves to them, that is, become proselytes to their religion, to observe them. He quotes the rabbinic canon that binds every class to the keeping of the day: all are obliged to read the Megillah, the book of Esther, priests and Levites and Israelites, men and women and proselytes and freed servants, and the little ones are trained up to read it too.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch give the force of the words: the Jews ordained and took upon themselves, their seed, and all who should join them, so that it should not fail, inviolably, to keep these two days according to their writing and their appointed time every year. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley explains why the proselytes were included: as Gentile converts they were obliged to the other Jewish laws and therefore to this, and the rather because they had shared in the very deliverance the day commemorates, without which the Jewish nation and religion had been in great measure, if not wholly, extinct.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse widens the feast beyond the bounds of blood. Purim is laid not on the living generation only but on all their descendants, and not on the natural Israel only but on every stranger who casts in his lot with the covenant people; the deliverance that saved the nation is to be remembered by all who share the nation's life. Wesley's point gives the reason its weight: the proselytes owed their own standing to the same rescue, for had Haman prevailed there would have been no people for them to join. So the keeping of the day becomes a mark of belonging: to remember Purim is to confess oneself among the delivered, and the feast binds together, in one perpetual thanksgiving, both the children of Israel and all who have joined themselves to Israel's God. Gill's rabbinic canon, binding priest and Levite, man and woman, proselyte and freedman alike to read the Megillah, Keil and Delitzsch's inviolable ordinance laid on the seed for ever, and Wesley's reason that the proselytes too were saved by this deliverance, together widen the day past every boundary of blood and generation. Had Haman prevailed, Wesley reminds us, there had been no nation for any stranger to join; the feast therefore gathers into one company all whose very standing hangs upon the mercy it commemorates.
28:
The ordinance is pressed to its furthest extent, every generation, every family, every province, every city, and the witnesses weigh the reach of the remembrance. The reformed John Gill observes that the days are indeed commemorated still, by all the families of the Jews and by all in them capable of it; and he draws from Aben Ezra the reason for the piling up of "every province" and "every city": the words are added lest a man should think himself excused from keeping the feast where there are no other Jews, for, be he where he may, he is bound to observe it. Keil and Delitzsch, the grammatical-historical voices, render the clause with its double guarantee, that these days should be remembered and kept throughout every generation, and that they should never fail from among the Jews nor their memorial perish from their seed, the participles carrying the sense of an observance made perpetual and inviolable.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gives the ground of so anxious a permanence: the memorial of the great things God had done for his church was never to perish from their seed, for God does not work wonders for a day, but to be had in everlasting remembrance, what he does is for ever, as in Eccl. 3:14, and should therefore for ever be kept in mind. In this feast, Henry notes, the Jews would remember Haman's malice to his perpetual reproach, Esther's good service to her lasting honour, and their own prayers and the answers given them.

The witnesses do not divide, and together they make the verse a meditation on why God's people keep their festivals at all. A deliverance unremembered is a deliverance half-lost; and so the mercy is fenced about with every safeguard language can raise, every generation, every family, every place, that no Jew, however isolated, and no age, however distant, should let the memory lapse. The care is not superstition but gratitude taught to endure: what God did once for a doomed people is to be told and retold until it belongs as surely to the children's children as to those who first felt the sword lifted from their necks. Gill's note from Aben Ezra, that the isolated Jew is bound no less than the crowded city, Keil and Delitzsch's double guarantee that the memorial shall never fail nor perish, and Henry's insistence that God works no wonder merely for a day, all press toward the one end, a mercy fenced round with every safeguard against forgetting. The witnesses make the heaping of the words, every generation, family, province, and city, not a lawyer's excess but the anxiety of gratitude to endure.
29:
A second and weightier letter goes out, and the witnesses note both its authors and the puzzle of its numbering. The reformed John Gill explains the need for it: before, Mordecai had only recommended the feast, but now Esther the queen adds her sanction and lays her obligation upon the Jews, perhaps because some had been backward or negligent in observing it, so that queen and minister join to press it home. He records that by the Jewish reckoning this was written the year following, and that the former Targum takes it to mean they set the whole miraculous deliverance in its strongest light. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render "with all authority" as "with all strength," that is, very forcibly, to give the contents of this letter the force of law; and they call it the "second" with reference to Mordecai's first letter of v.20.

Here the witnesses divide over what the second letter is second to. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott judges that the first letter must be the one Esther had extracted from the king in Esther 8:8, so that this second letter is Mordecai's of v.20, now confirmed in a more authoritative way. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads it otherwise: the former letter of v.20 only recommended the feast, while this present one enjoins it, being now not Mordecai's act alone but the act of all the Jews binding themselves and their posterity. Clarke, the other wesleyan-arminian voice, adds simply that Esther and Mordecai had the king's licence for what they did, and that their own authority was great and extensive.

The witnesses do not let the numbering obscure the point. Whether this is the second letter after the king's or the second after Mordecai's first recommendation, all agree on its function: to raise the observance of Purim from a warm suggestion to a binding decree, backed now by the queen's name as well as the minister's. What had been proposed is here commanded, and commanded with all the weight that royal and official authority could lend it, that a feast begun in gratitude might stand as a settled and unbreakable law among the people. Gill supposes the queen's fuller sanction was needed because some had grown backward in the keeping; Keil and Delitzsch render the phrase as writing with all strength, to give the letter the force of law; and though Ellicott and Wesley part over which letter is reckoned the first, none doubts that this one was meant to bind. So the witnesses let the doubled authorship, queen and minister together, seal an observance that a single voice had only recommended.
30:
The letters are dispatched across the whole empire, and the witnesses attend to their reach and their tone. The reformed John Gill notes that it was Mordecai who sent them, signed in the queen's name and his own. Keil and Delitzsch, the grammatical-historical witnesses, give the compass of the mailing: copies of the writing were sent to all the Jews in the hundred and twenty-seven provinces of the kingdom of Ahasuerus, "words of peace and truth," that is, letters containing words of peace and truth, to appoint the days of Purim in their seasons, as Mordecai and Esther had enjoined and as the Jews had taken upon themselves and their descendants, together with the matters of the fastings and their lamentations.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley unfolds the two qualities named: the letters went out with "peace," that is with friendship and kindness toward his brethren, and with "truth," that is with sincerity. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott offers only a small correction of the rendering, that the article should be dropped, not "the letters" but simply "letters."

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse quietly enlarges the feast to the full breadth of the dispersion. Purim is not to be a local memory of Susa or of a few provinces, but the common inheritance of Jews in all the hundred and twenty-seven provinces over which the decree of death had once run; the same empire-wide reach that had carried Haman's edict of extermination now carries Mordecai's edict of remembrance. And the character of the letters is itself a token of the deliverance: where the first writing had gone out with words of destruction, these go out with words of peace and truth, kindness to the brethren and sincerity of heart. The witnesses let the contrast stand, the machinery of a hostile state, once bent to a people's ruin, now bearing to every province the settled and gentle news that they are saved, and bidding them keep the memory in peace. Keil and Delitzsch trace the full errand, copies to all the hundred and twenty-seven provinces, appointing the days in their seasons as Esther and Mordecai had enjoined and the people had taken on themselves, with the matters of fasting and lamentation joined to the joy; Gill marks the letters signed in the queen's name and his own; Wesley reads peace and truth as kindness and sincerity; Ellicott mends only the article. That every province touched by Haman's edict of death should be reached again by Mordecai's edict of remembrance is itself a token of the completeness of the reversal, the whole apparatus of the state turned from the ruin of the Jews to the keeping of their feast.
31:
The letters fix not only a feast but a fast, and the witnesses attend to the joining of the two. The reformed John Gill reads the aim plainly: to confirm these days of Purim in their appointed times, the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar. Keil and Delitzsch, the grammatical-historical voices, give the fuller clause, to confirm the days as Mordecai the Jew and Esther the queen had enjoined, and as the Jews had decreed for themselves and for their seed, together with "the matters of the fastings and their cry." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes that a single Hebrew verb underlies the English "confirm," "enjoin," and "decree," the same word as the "stablish" of v.21, meaning to fix or settle; and he observes that the phrase about the fastings and their cry comes in somewhat awkwardly and is passed over by the Septuagint, so that some have doubted its genuineness, yet all Hebrew manuscripts and the other ancient versions keep it, and it is best taken to mean that the Jews had instituted fasts and lamentations in addition to what Mordecai's letter enjoined, which he connects with the fast still observed on the thirteenth of Adar.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley explains the "cry": it looks back to the great calamities that had been decreed against all the Jews, for the removing of which not Esther and the Jews of Shushan only, but all the Jews everywhere, had fled to God by fasting and strong cries. The fast, that is, remembers the terror out of which the feast was born.

The witnesses do not divide, and together they show a people whose thanksgiving does not forget its tears. The days of Purim are fixed with feasting for the deliverance, but with fasting too for the danger; the joy is anchored in the memory of the cry that went up when the danger was fresh. Ellicott's small textual doubt only serves to highlight how firmly the tradition held the two together, so that the very calendar of the feast keeps a day of grief beside its days of gladness, the fast of the thirteenth before the feasts of the fourteenth and fifteenth, lest the delivered forget from what depth they were raised. Gill fixes the days, Keil and Delitzsch join the fasting and the cry to Esther and Mordecai's injunction, Ellicott weighs and keeps the disputed clause, and Wesley traces the cry to the strong supplications that had gone up when the danger was fresh; together they show a feast that carries its own fast within it. The joy of Purim is never cut loose from the grief it answers, and the calendar itself preserves the memory of the tears.
32:
The chapter closes on the decree of Esther and a phrase that has long puzzled interpreters, "and it was written in the book." The reformed John Gill reads the first clause simply: the decree of Esther confirmed these matters of Purim, establishing the festival to be observed by the Jews in all future generations. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke adds that her decree was received universally and with all respect, the Jews binding themselves to abide by it; he notes the Vulgate's expansive turn, "all things which are contained in the history of this book, which is called Esther," and the Targum's rendering, that by Esther's word these matters were confirmed and the roll transcribed in this book.

Over the closing words the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott opens a genuine question: it is doubtful what "the book" here means. The Vulgate and many moderns explain it of the book of Esther itself; but "the book," Ellicott objects, hardly seems a natural Hebrew way for an author to refer to the very work he is writing, and no like case can be adduced. Others suppose a book written at the time on the subject of the festival, which he grants is possible; while Canon Rawlinson would identify it with the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Media and Persia, since that is how the word "book" is used elsewhere in Esther. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley takes it more modestly still, as the records the Jews kept of their most memorable passages.

The witnesses do not resolve the question, and they do not need to. Whether the book be Esther's own scroll, a lost record of the feast, or the royal Persian annals, the point the verse makes is the same: the decree of the queen did not die with the moment but was set down in writing, that it might stand. And with that act of writing the whole story comes to rest, a deliverance first lived, then commemorated in a feast, then bound upon the people by letter, and at last committed to a book, so that what God had done should be neither forgotten by the generation that saw it nor hidden from the generations that had not. The chapter that opened with a decree of death closes with a decree of remembrance, written down to endure. Gill and Clarke read the queen's decree confirmed and universally received, Ellicott canvasses the several senses of the book, Esther's own scroll, a lost record of the feast, or the Persian chronicles, and Wesley takes it for the Jews' register of their memorable passages; but the witnesses agree that the point lies not in the puzzle but in the writing. What the queen decreed was set down that it might stand, and the deliverance passes at last from living memory into a book, secured against the forgetfulness of the generations that had not seen it.
